label: digit 3 fed back as input during the copy phase
explanation: Fires only in the copy phase (t > L) when the input token is the digit 3, i.e. when the model's own previously-emitted 3 is fed back in. All activation mass falls on these steps (recall 1.0); it never fires on 3 in the original phase or at the delimiter, and never on any other input token. About 18% of copy-phase 3 inputs stay inactive. Magnitude is largest when the 3 comes early in the copy (3 as original token 1, fed back at recall_idx 2; the top examples are all this case, up to 3.67) and is small when the 3 comes late in the copy. Activation rate is higher in sequences that contain more digits.

issues: The core claims hold. On the dev split every activation is in the copy phase with in_tok == '3' (0 activations in the original or delimiter phases, 0 on other tokens). On the test split the misses run found 0 missed activations. Test precision is 0.815, recall 1.0, F1 0.898.

The false positives follow a pattern, but it is a small one. When the 3 is fed back at recall_idx 1 (the 3 was original token 0), precision is 0.68, compared with 0.95 at recall_idx 2 and 0.94 at recall_idx 3. This depends strongly on L: precision is 0.036 at L=3, 0.27 at L=4, 0.54 at L=5 and 0.72 at L=6. Over all copy-phase 3s with L=3 the feature almost never fires (precision 0.047, 42 activations in total).

Late copy positions are also weaker: precision is 0.73 for recall_idx >= 5 and 0.70 for to_go == 0. This is a gradual fall-off, not a clean exception, so it fits the explanation's 'activations are small when the 3 comes late'.

Supporting claims check out. Activation mass peaks at recall_idx 2 (31.5%), which matches the top-example claim. The digit-count effect is real but small: precision is 0.80 with n_digits == 1 and 0.84 with n_digits >= 3.

The explanation says about 18% of copy-phase 3s stay inactive but does not say where they are. They cluster in short sequences where the 3 was the first token, and in late copy positions. Excluding the short-sequence cases raises test F1 only slightly (0.898 to 0.908), so the original predicate is still adequate.
